definition: Surmise means to infer something from little evidence.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word surmise. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know surmise should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When the elevator kept stopping at three, Rosa surmised that the new tenant was moving in load by load.
A pure guess is weaker than a surmise: a guess may rest on nothing at all, while a surmise at least grows from a few real clues.
Deduce goes further than surmise: a deduction locks each clue into a firm chain of reasoning, while a surmise leaps carefully from scraps.

To infer is to draw a conclusion from evidence — any evidence, thin or overwhelming; the word itself says nothing about how much. Surmise is the special case at the thin end: a surmise is an inference built on scraps and held loosely, because so little is holding it up.

Gather is the offhand, informal word for reading hints — 'I gather you're leaving' — a mild conclusion picked up in passing, nothing checked and nothing chained together. A surmise takes the hints more seriously: it weighs each scrap and offers, carefully, the conclusion they point to.

Surmise is the honest verb for this conclusion — drawn from scraps, stated with care, and one storm-soaked ledger away from being overturned.

A surmise stands exactly in between.

The shoebox from Aunt Ruth's attic held no diary, only fragments: three ticket stubs, a pressed flower, and one postcard signed with the letter M.
From these scraps, Nora could only surmise the outline of a story.
The stubs were all for the same island steamer, in three different springs; the flower was a variety that grows on the island the steamer serves.
So she offered her conclusion carefully, holding it loosely: Ruth had crossed each year to meet someone, and M had mattered.
But when Nora found the island's name inked faintly on the box lid, the thin little theory grew a spine.
